issues.legal_issue: An appellate court reviewing a trial court’s finding based on conflicting oral testimony should give due weight to the trial court’s opportunity to observe the witnesses and should not reverse without a sufficient reason.
material_facts: The adoption finding turned principally on conflicting oral testimony, with a few documents supplementing that testimony.
The trial court analysed the material witnesses and relied in part on its observation of their demeanour, while weighing the evidence against the surrounding facts and probabilities.
The appellate court reversed the finding, but its assessment was affected by errors in evaluating the evidence and did not disclose an adequate ground to displace the trial court’s finding.
issues.conclusion: The appellate court had no adequate ground to reverse the trial court’s finding on adoption; the trial court’s finding was restored.
issues.legal_principle: The principle is one of practice governing the weight accorded to a trial court’s factual finding on oral evidence: where credibility is in issue, the trial court’s advantage in seeing and hearing witnesses should be respected unless a special feature was overlooked, improbability sufficiently displaces its view, or its appraisal is materially irregular, relies on inadmissible evidence, misreads the evidence, or rests on conjecture or surmise. The Court relied on W.C. Macdonald v. Fred Latimer, Watt v. Thomas, Sara Veeraswami alias Sara Veerraju v. Talluri Narayya, Sarju Parshad v. Raja Jwaleshwari Pratap Narain Singh, and The Asiatic Steam Navigation Co. Ltd. v. Sub-Lt. Arabinda Chakravarti.

rule.if: appeal_from_trial_finding and oral_credibility_dispute and trial_court_observed_witnesses and not overlooked_material_feature and not sufficient_improbability and not material_appraisal_error

predicates.appeal_from_trial_finding: A party appealed from a trial court’s finding of fact.
predicates.oral_credibility_dispute: The finding depended on resolving conflicting oral testimony by assessing witness credibility.
predicates.trial_court_observed_witnesses: The trial court heard the witnesses and observed their demeanour while they testified.
predicates.overlooked_material_feature: A material feature of a witness’s evidence escaped the trial court’s notice.
predicates.sufficient_improbability: The evidence contained a sufficient balance of improbability to displace the trial court’s view of credibility.
predicates.material_appraisal_error: The trial court’s appraisal was materially irregular, relied on inadmissible evidence, misread evidence, or rested on conjecture or surmise.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a trial court’s credibility finding on conflicting oral testimony, and the trial court observed the witnesses without an overlooked material feature, sufficient improbability, or material appraisal error, the trial court’s finding should prevail.

issues.legal_issue: A court cannot reject a witness’s testimony solely because the witness is related to the party who called the witness or may be prejudiced against the opposing party.
material_facts: The appellate court substantially rejected the testimony of witnesses because they were related to the claimant or were said to be out of favour with the opposing side.
The trial court had considered the witnesses’ testimony in light of the surrounding circumstances and the full body of evidence.
The appellate court did not give adequate weight to the nature and probability of the evidence in the context of the record as a whole.
issues.conclusion: Relationship or possible prejudice alone did not justify rejecting the witnesses’ testimony; it had to be assessed cautiously against the entire record.
issues.legal_principle: A witness’s relationship to the party producing the witness, or possible prejudice against the opposing party, calls for appropriate caution in assessing probative value. It does not, by itself, justify rejecting the testimony; the evidence must be considered in the context of the entire mosaic of facts on the record.

predicates.witness_relationship_or_possible_prejudi: A witness was related to the party who called the witness or could be prejudiced against the opposing party.
predicates.evidence_assessable_in_record_context: The witness’s testimony could be assessed alongside the other evidence and surrounding circumstances in the case.

issues.definition: When a witness is related to the calling party or may be prejudiced against the opposing party, the testimony must be assessed in the context of the record, and that relationship or possible prejudice alone does not justify rejecting it.

issues.legal_issue: A claimed adoption that would displace natural succession must be proved as a fact, and a valid adoption requires the actual physical giving and acceptance of the child; an additional ceremony is required only when the applicable law or custom makes it necessary.
material_facts: The claimant asserted that he had been adopted by a childless couple and relied on oral testimony about the adoption and the physical act of giving and taking.
The trial court found the adoption proved after considering the testimony, an adoption deed signed by the couple, other documents, and the circumstances surrounding the adoption.

The appellate court rejected the adoption, but its assessment failed to account for material evidence and applied a standard of proof unsuited to circumstances in which the adoptive mother was seriously ill and elaborate arrangements were not feasible.

The evidence supported the trial court’s finding that the physical act of adoption occurred; the claimant relied on a community custom under which giving and taking sufficed, and no evidence showed that an additional fire ceremony was necessary.
issues.conclusion: The adoption was proved in fact and was valid; the trial court’s finding was restored.
issues.legal_principle: A person alleging adoption to displace natural succession bears the burden of proving both the factum and validity of the adoption, and the evidence must be free from suspicion and consistent and probable, but adoption is proved in the same way as any other fact. Actual delivery and acceptance of the child is an essential requisite in every adoption, notwithstanding consent or a deed. No particular form is prescribed for giving and taking. A datta homam is not necessary where the applicable custom suffices or, for the twice-born classes, where the adopted boy belongs to the adoptive father’s gotra. The Court relied on A. Raghavamma v. A. Chenchamma, Kishori Lal v. Chaltibai, Shoshinath v. Krishnasunder, Lakshman Singh v. Smt. Rupkanwar, and Bal Gangadhar Tilak v. Shrinivas Pandit; it also considered Sutroogan v. Sabitra concerning suspicious circumstances and proof.

rule.if: adoption_claim_in_succession_dispute and actual_giving_and_acceptance and reliable_contextual_proof and no_evidence_additional_rite_required

predicates.adoption_claim_in_succession_dispute: A person claimed adoption as a basis for displacing the ordinary course of succession to property.
predicates.actual_giving_and_acceptance: The child was physically delivered by the natural parent and accepted by the adoptive parent as part of an adoption ceremony.
predicates.reliable_contextual_proof: The evidence of adoption was consistent and probable when assessed against the surrounding circumstances and the whole record.
predicates.no_evidence_additional_rite_required: The record did not show that an additional religious ceremony was required under the applicable custom or circumstances.

issues.definition: When a succession dispute involves a claim of adoption, the child was physically given and accepted, the contextual evidence is reliable, and no additional rite is shown to be required, the adoption is proved and valid.

issues.legal_issue: A member of a joint Hindu family effects separation by clearly communicating an unequivocal intention to separate to the co-sharer affected; an uncommunicated declaration does not effect separation.
material_facts: A trust deed contained a declaration of an intention to separate if the adoption were held valid.
The declaration was conditional and was not communicated to the co-sharer whose interest would be affected.
There was no evidence that the co-sharer otherwise learned of the intention to separate.
issues.conclusion: The declaration in the trust deed did not effect a partition or separation.
issues.legal_principle: Separation from a joint Hindu family requires a clear and unequivocal intimation of the member’s desire to separate to the co-sharers; a mere uncommunicated declaration is only an unexpressed intention. The Court relied on Girja Bai v. Sadashiv Dhundiraj, Bal Krishan v. Ram Krishan, A. Raghavamma v. A. Chenchamma, Puttrangamma v. M.S. Ranganna, and Kalyani v. Narayanan.

predicates.joint_family_separation_dispute: The dispute concerned whether a member had separated from a joint Hindu family.
predicates.unequivocal_intention_declared: A member made a clear and unequivocal declaration of an intention to separate.
predicates.intention_communicated_to_affected_co_sh: The member communicated the intention to separate to the co-sharer whose interest was affected.

issues.definition: In a joint family separation dispute, a clear declaration that was not communicated to the affected co-sharer does not effect separation.
